items.title: Tech sell-off resumes as euphoria from Jensen Huang’s Nvidia return subsides
items.summary:
Sell-off signals investors are bracing for further volatility in key AI sector driving economic growth worldwide

Technology shares led a market retreat Tuesday as caution returned after Jensen Huang’s extraordinary return to Nvidia days after he was forced to resign, with investors bracing for further volatility in a key sector driving economic growth worldwide.

A day after Huang’s reinstatement as CEO drove Nvidia shares up more than 30%, adding more than $900bn to the firm’s market value, the euphoria dissipated as its stock lost almost 6% by Tuesday’s close.

items.title: Compass’s logic for US listing is flimsy but UK ministers need to wake up to Footsie flight risk | Nils Pratley
items.summary:
The contract caterer switching to New York is a big hit to the London Stock Exchange but what is being done to discourage others from delisting?

That’s gratitude, eh? Compass Group built its business, in part, on contracts to serve dinners in British schools and run catering operations in NHS hospitals. Now it plans to switch its primary stock market listing to New York in 2028.

Compass is a bad one for the London market to lose. First, it is the 18th largest company in the FTSE 100 index and one of the few that is the biggest in the world in its market (contract catering, not just for the public sector but for thousands of corporate clients). Second, its reasons for joining the stateside listing rush feel flimsy – but also dangerous.

Continue reading...

items.title: Trump made up to $15m on Nvidia stock after Huang’s return
items.summary:
US president says he ‘convinced’ chipmaker’s board to reinstate CEO, as Nvidia shares fall after previous day’s rally

  • Nvidia staff: what do you think of Jensen Huang’s return as chief executive?

Donald Trump made up to $15m (£11.5m) on his holdings of Nvidia stock after the US chipmaker’s share price soared on the surprise return of Jensen Huang as chief executive.

Huang, who co-founded the company in 1993, was ousted by the board after allegations that he had three affairs, including one with a suspected Chinese spy and two with employees. But the Nvidia board reinstated him after an intervention from the US president.

items.title: Mamdani says Nvidia drama shows stock market is overly dependent on AI
items.summary:
New York City mayor notes ‘massive impact’ on working Americans’ lives when Jensen Huang stepped down as CEO

Zohran Mamdani, New York City’s mayor, on Monday weighed in on the corporate turbulence surrounding Nvidia and the chipmaker’s chief executive officer, Jensen Huang, saying he does not think working Americans “signed up for their pensions being tied to the question of … Huang’s fidelity to his marriage”.

The mayor said Huang “had a massive impact”, with Nvidia’s share price dropping dramatically when Huang stepped down as the company’s CEO on 12 November after a reported extramarital relationship with a suspected Chinese spy.

Continue reading...

items.summary:
New value still half a trillion dollars lower than before affair was revealed; Trump hails Huang as a ‘great patriot and national treasure’

  • Jensen Huang reinstated as Nvidia CEO

  • Timeline: fall and comeback of Jensen Huang

Shares in UK housebuilder Crest Nicholson have slumped by a quarter, to a record low, after the company issued a profits warning this morning.

Full year completions were 1,353, at the bottom end of the Group’s previous guidance range of 1,350 to 1,400 completions.

The warning has hammered Crest Nicholson shares, which have lost more than a quarter of their value this morning, currently trading down over 30%. The brutal sell-off is also weighing on the wider sector, dragging peers like Barratt Redrow, Persimmon, Vistry and Bellway into the red.

Today’s update suggests that weakness in the housing market is no longer confined to first-time buyers. Crest Nicholson is predominantly exposed to the mid-premium family housing market, and the sharp deterioration in sales rates indicates that more affluent upsizers are also becoming increasingly cautious amid macroeconomic and geopolitical uncertainty.

It has been a volatile time on global stock markets, with rapid rallies and punishing sell-offs. There have been signs in recent weeks that investors are getting cold feet over the outlook for AI companies and selling off technology stocks.

items.title: Anthropic’s IPO was great for the tech elite – and not so great for the rest of us | Steven Greenhouse
items.summary:
The company’s co-founders are now wildly rich, while countless Americans face AI-driven threats to their jobs and fears of a stock bubble

The sultans of Silicon Valley and the wizards of Wall Street rejoiced this week when Anthropic raised an eye-popping $81bn in the largest initial public offering in history. They saw the AI company’s IPO as a gung-ho affirmation of Silicon Valley’s and Wall Street’s marriage of technology and capitalism.

For many employees at the company that developed Claude, the public offering must have been a thing of dreams. With the IPO valuing Anthropic at $1.5tn, the company’s seven co-founders each came away with stakes worth about $20bn, while, by one estimate, 600 of Anthropic’s more than 5,000 employees will have holdings topping $100m and 2,800 others will have shares worth more than $10m.

items.summary:
The Nasdaq lost trillions in value, with the AI startup’s IPO failing to buoy it as investors question huge sums being poured into AI buildout

  • Who are Anthropic’s seven co-founders, now worth $180bn?

As Anthropic’s stock dropped during its second day of trading, the wider stock market dipped with it. On Friday, the Nasdaq Composite erased all its gains for 2026 and closed down 5% from its value on 1 January. The Dow Jones Industrial Average and S&P 500 closed in correction territory.

Anthropic’s record-breaking IPO failed to stem a global sell-off in AI-linked companies, and the tech-heavy Nasdaq erased some $4tn in market value this week, according to the Wall Street Journal.

items.summary:
Rolling coverage of the latest economic and financial news

California has served an investigative subpoena on Nvidia after a scandal that prompted the departure of co-founder and longtime chief executive Jensen Huang.

Rob Bonta, the US state’s attorney general, issued the subpoena as part of an investigation into whether exports of the California-based company’s advanced semiconductor chips ended up in China, contravening US restrictions.

The conduct of Nvidia and its former chief executive raises bright red flags, including about the ways in which the company may have misled investors.

Nvidia is in a messy, transnational situation but the underlying principle of our corporate securities law is clear: Companies cannot mislead their investors.”

items.title: Anthropic’s historic stock market debut: key takeaways, and what comes next for the AI industry
items.summary:
A record breaking IPO has raised billions for the AI frontier lab – but experts say the coming months could prove bumpy, as the industry faces a variety of challenges

  • Anthropic closes first day of public trading at $1.3tn valuation after largest-ever IPO

In the end, Anthropic’s much-anticipated IPO more than lived up to the hype. The market’s embrace of one of the AI industry’s most talked about companies has resulted in the maker of the Claude chatbot becoming one of the world’s most valuable firms after just one day of trading.

With many of the company’s founders, investors and employees now worth billions of dollars – and demand for the company’s stock remaining resilient – attention now turns to the stability of the wider market, and the global headwinds that experts say could threaten the AI industry over the coming months.

Continue reading...
items.t: Anthropic’s historic stock market debut: key takeaways, and what comes next for the AI industry
